intro:
A time of day behind a trigger, in one of three faces.

The value is `{ hour, minute }` on a 24-hour clock whatever the face shows. A 12-hour display is a rendering choice; storing 7pm as `{ hour: 7 }` plus a meridiem flag would put that flag into every comparison downstream.

The three layouts exist because "pick a time" is three tasks. `wheel` is the precise one — any minute in the day is two or three flicks away. `clock` picks a *slot* rather than a time, and answers "morning or evening?" faster than digits. `ruler` is the coarse one, and the only one that reads at arm's length.

All three produce the same value and take the same props, so swapping between them is a one-word change. For a day and a time together, use [DateTimePicker](/docs/components/date-time-picker).

parts.Trigger: Wraps a trigger of your own and opens the panel on press. Pass a child to the picker instead and it is wrapped for you.

examples.title: A time
examples.description: The trigger reads back the chosen time and falls back to the placeholder. Nothing chosen yet means the wheel opens near the current hour rather than at midnight — an unset picker still has to open somewhere plausible.

examples.title: A 24-hour clock
examples.description: `hourCycle={24}` drops the meridiem column entirely and writes hours 00–23. The stored value does not change: it was always on a 24-hour clock.

examples.title: Slots, not times
examples.description: A `minuteStep` turns the wheel into a list of the times you actually offer. Half-hour slots is four rows of scrolling instead of sixty.

examples.title: Within opening hours
examples.description: `minTime` and `maxTime` bound the value rather than the scroll. A face reports the row it landed on and the picker clamps it, so every layout is bounded by the same rule and a value outside the span comes back as the nearest one inside it.
examples.code:
<TimePicker
  value={time}
  onValueChange={setTime}
  minTime={{ hour: 9, minute: 0 }}
  maxTime={{ hour: 17, minute: 30 }}
  minuteStep={15}
/>

examples.title: The clock face
examples.description: A face beside a list of times. The hands sweep to the selection rather than jumping, because the face’s whole job is to say *when in the day* the highlighted row is — and a hand that jumps gives that away one row at a time.

examples.title: The ruler, in a sheet
examples.description: One large readout over a scale you swipe. It is the layout that reads at arm's length, so it is the one for a sheet — where the panel takes the full width and the Done button with it, because a sheet's outside is only the strip above it.

previewVideo.alt: TimePicker — The ruler, in a sheet.

examples.title: The four presentations
examples.description: `presentation` decides where the picker opens, and the choice is about how much of the screen the answer is worth. `popover` keeps the field in view and is the default; `dialog` takes the middle of the screen for a choice that is the whole point of the step; `bottom-sheet` puts it under the thumb, which is what a scale you swipe wants; and `inline` opens nothing at all, for a picker that is part of a form rather than behind it.
examples.code:
<TimePicker presentation="popover" value={time} onValueChange={setTime} />
<TimePicker presentation="dialog" … />
<TimePicker presentation="bottom-sheet" … />
<TimePicker presentation="inline" … />

examples.title: In a dialog
examples.description: The same panel over a frosted screen. Worth it when the time *is* the decision on the screen — the blur says that in a way a dim does not, and falls back to the dim where expo-blur is not installed.

examples.title: Inline, inside a Frame
examples.description: `inline` renders the panel with no trigger and no overlay, so it can be composed into a card of your own. The toggle goes outside the card: it chooses *which* time the card is editing, which is a decision about the card rather than a control inside it.
examples.code:
const [edge, setEdge] = useState('start');

<View className="gap-3">
  <ToggleButtonGroup
    selectionMode="single"
    size="sm"
    value={[edge]}
    onValueChange={(next) => setEdge(next[0] ?? 'start')}
    className="w-full justify-between px-1"
  >
    <ToggleButton id="start">Starts</ToggleButton>
    <ToggleButton id="end">Ends</ToggleButton>
  </ToggleButtonGroup>

  <Frame>
    <Frame.Header>
      <Frame.Title>Time</Frame.Title>
      <Frame.Action>
        {formatTime(start)} – {formatTime(end)}
      </Frame.Action>
    </Frame.Header>
    <Frame.Panel>
      <Frame.Section className="items-center">
        <TimePicker
          presentation="inline"
          layout="clock"
          value={edge === 'start' ? start : end}
          onValueChange={edge === 'start' ? setStart : setEnd}
        />
      </Frame.Section>
    </Frame.Panel>
  </Frame>
</View>

examples.title: Your own trigger
examples.description: Pass a child and it is cloned with an `onPress` that opens the panel, so a field row or an icon button can stand in for the default button.
examples.code:
<TimePicker value={time} onValueChange={setTime}>
  <Button variant="ghost" size="icon" accessibilityLabel="Choose a time">
    <ClockIcon size={18} />
  </Button>
</TimePicker>

examples.title: Turning the readout down
examples.description: The `ruler` face states its time in one large centred number, which is right when the scale is the only thing on the panel. Under something that outranks it — a calendar, a form row — that number is the largest text on screen standing for the smaller half of the answer. `compact` steps it down; `none` drops it, for a caller writing the time itself. The other two faces spell the time out in their own columns and hands and ignore this.
examples.code:
<TimePicker layout="ruler" readout="compact" value={time} onValueChange={setTime} />

{/* …or take it over entirely */}
<TimePicker presentation="inline" layout="ruler" readout="none" … />

notes:
**The value is always 0–23.** `displayHour` and `hourFromDisplay` are exported alongside it if you need the face's own numbering, but nothing stored should be in it.

**`minuteStep` defaults per layout.** `wheel` steps by 1, `clock` by 30 and `ruler` by 15 — the two that scroll the whole day at once need a coarser grid to be usable. Pass it explicitly and the layout stops mattering.

**A chosen time off the step is rounded, not rejected.** At a 30-minute step 7:29 is a finger that stopped just short of half past, not a request for seven o'clock.

**Every face is a scroll view.** Momentum, deceleration and fling physics come from the platform, and the selection is the row it comes to rest on. That is also why the panel needs a definite width, which the presentations give it.

**The sheet gets a Done button and the popover does not.** A popover is dismissed by tapping anywhere outside it, which is most of the screen; a sheet's outside is the strip above it, and a scale under your thumb needs somewhere deliberate to finish.
